text.p: The Colombian government has raised the political stakes in the issue of British Petroleum Co Ltd's contract for the condensate-rich Piedemonte block by granting special decision-making powers to Congress.
The British oil giant has been involved in a protracted wrangle with state-run oil company Ecopetrol and the government over the terms of how profits from the field should be divided up.
This week Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar, on orders from President Ernesto Samper, said Congress would have the last word on fixing the government's position.

"Congress will have the last word in fixing Ecopetrol and the government's position since no solution was possible through legal or technical means. This will be politicizing the subject," a spokeswoman for the Mines and Energy Ministry told Reuters Thursday.

Villamizar was said to be "worried" about throwing a contractual issue into political terrain but told reporters Thursday: "If we're stuck to the contract then Piedemonte will not be exploited with high costs for the nation and for the foreign company."

BP's Colombian unit BP Exploration maintains the long-running Piedemonte dispute is twofold -- firstly, the interpretation of what the principal hydrocarbon is and secondly how to boost its long-term profit margins.

A BP spokesman referred to the latest twist in the Piedemonte saga, saying: "There are still some legal differences but there have been significant approximations at least in terms of developing Piedemonte-1."
"Contacts are being maintained because it's clear that any contractual differences must be resolved by signatories to the contract which are BP and Ecopetrol," he added.
He said if the decision reached by Congress was not acceptable to BP then it could take the matter to an arbitration panel.

Reserves in the formations so far discovered in the Piedemonte block -- Florena, Pauto and Volcanera, which cover about 15 percent of the total area -- are estimated at one billion barrels of condensates and 10 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
Commercial operations have not yet started at the field but BP has been pushing for the sliding scale contract, which determines how profits are split with Ecopetrol, to be driven by gas.

Taking gas as the principal hydrocarbon would boost short- term profitability since it would take longer to reach the upper end of the scale, according to which Ecopetrol takes 70 percent of profits once total production surpasses 150 million barrels of crude equivalent.

In order to boost the long-term profitability of the 85 percent of the field so far unexplored, BP has been pushing for sweeter contract terms, possibly even a switch to a shared-risk factor contract, under which Ecopetrol would share exploration costs.
